hypotheses.claim: Changing `matches(String)` to `matches(String...)` removes the JVM-level `matches(String)` method, so previously compiled plugins or modules invoking that public method may fail at runtime with `NoSuchMethodError`.
hypotheses.why_suspected: Java varargs compile as an array parameter, changing the descriptor from `(String)` to `(String[])`; the evidence shows direct replacement rather than retaining a forwarding single-name overload.
questions_to_resolve: Is `DBSObjectFilter` part of the binary compatibility contract for independently compiled DBeaver plugins?
Are any distributed or third-party binaries compiled against `matches(String)`?

hypotheses.claim: Multi-name filtering may reject an overloaded object even when one candidate identity satisfies the complete filter, because inclusion matching one name and exclusion matching a different name is evaluated as a rejection rather than evaluating each candidate identity independently.
hypotheses.why_suspected: The implementation computes `any name matches an include` and then rejects on `any name matches an exclude`. Thus, for example, an overloaded name can satisfy the include while the ordinary name independently satisfies an exclude, although the included identity itself is not excluded.
questions_to_resolve: Is the intended contract `exists name: include(name) && !exclude(name)`, or should an exclusion matching any alias reject the whole object?
What results are expected when include and exclude patterns match different identities of the same overloaded object?

outcomes.supported_claim: The change replaces the public one-argument source signature with a varargs/array signature in an exported package, and another plugin’s source calls the former one-argument API. The evidence does not establish that any previously compiled binary containing that invocation will actually be loaded with the changed class.
outcomes.reasoning: The diff shows `matches(String)` being replaced by `matches(String...)`, which changes the JVM parameter type from `String` to `String[]`. L2 shows that `org.jkiss.dbeaver.model.struct` is exported, and E15 shows a caller in a separate plugin source tree. These facts support a binary-compatibility risk. However, E15 is source evidence, not evidence of a distributed stale binary, and it will compile against the new varargs method when rebuilt. No supplied evidence identifies an existing distributed or third-party binary compiled against the old descriptor, nor shows that bundle resolution permits such an old consumer to run with the new provider. Therefore an actual `NoSuchMethodError` path cannot be established or ruled out.
outcomes.causal_link: If a pre-change consumer binary invokes `DBSObjectFilter.matches` with the old `String` descriptor and is loaded with this changed class, replacing that method with the `String[]` varargs method removes the exact target and would cause linkage failure. The evidence does not establish that such a stale consumer binary is present or loadable in the affected distribution.

outcomes.supported_claim: Conditionally, for an overloaded navigator object whose ordinary and overloaded names differ, if an include pattern matches one supplied name and an exclude pattern matches the other, DBSObjectFilter.matches returns false.
outcomes.reasoning: The changed implementation establishes the reported cross-name behavior: inclusion succeeds when any supplied name matches, while a later exclusion rejects when any supplied name matches. The navigator change supplies both the ordinary and overloaded names. However, the evidence does not establish that this behavior violates the intended filter contract; no specification or test says exclusions must be evaluated independently per candidate identity rather than applying to the whole object. The evidence also does not demonstrate a concrete overloaded object whose two supplied names differ. Therefore the behavior is supported conditionally, but its status as a defect cannot be concluded.
outcomes.causal_link: Before this change, the navigator passed only getName(). The changed navigator passes getName() and getOverloadedName(), and the changed filter independently searches all supplied names for inclusion and exclusion. Consequently, an include match on one name can be followed by an exclusion match on the other and return false. Whether that newly introduced cross-name rejection is erroneous depends on the unstated contract.
